mcqs.question: A staff candidate tells a well-executed but purely IC-scoped conflict story (a disagreement over one code review comment). Is the story dishonest?
options: Yes, because staff candidates should only tell stories about cross-org scope
No, but it answers a smaller-scope question than the level being interviewed for, since the same archetype needs a bigger radius of effect at staff level
Yes, because staff-level interviewers only accept stories with quantified metrics
No, and scope has no bearing on how the story is scored at any level
mcqs.explanation: The story can be entirely honest and well-told and still under-signal for the level, because staff loops are checking whether your typical scope matches the role — an accurate but small-scope story just answers a smaller version of the question than what's being assessed.

mcqs.question: A staff candidate cites 'reduced query time by 40% on my service' as their headline metric, with no broader context. Why might this under-signal at that level?
options: A 40% improvement is too small a number for any level
Metrics are not evaluated in staff-level behavioral rounds at all
The metric reflects magnitude on a single service, not radius of effect — staff-level signal usually comes from an outcome that changed how a team or org works, not just one service's number
It is fine and needs no additional context
mcqs.explanation: At senior/staff levels, interviewers look for the outcome's radius of effect — did the change spread beyond your own service to how a team or org operates — not just a bigger raw magnitude on a single, individually-owned metric.

mcqs.question: What's the recommended way to prepare a story that demonstrates 'the next level up' from your current target?
options: Exaggerate the scope of an existing story to make it sound bigger than it was
Skip this preparation — interviewers only evaluate your current level, never readiness for the next one
Find a real instance where you honestly operated with bigger scope than your day-to-day title implies, such as covering for an absent lead or driving a cross-team decision
Invent a hypothetical scenario and present it as if it happened
mcqs.explanation: The recommended approach is finding genuine, if occasional, instances of bigger scope you've actually lived through — not fabricating or exaggerating — since loops sometimes probe readiness for the next level, and a real (even if infrequent) example answers that directly.

mcqs.question: A strong IC keeps getting stuck at staff-level loops despite technically excellent, honest stories. What's the most likely underlying cause described in this topic?
options: The candidate is lying about their accomplishments and getting caught
The candidate's actual day-to-day work is still mostly IC-scoped, so their honest story bank doesn't contain cross-team or ambiguity-absorbing material the loop is checking for
The candidate is not using enough technical jargon in their answers
The interviewers are biased against individual contributors by design
mcqs.explanation: This pattern is usually not dishonesty — it reflects that the candidate's real day-to-day scope hasn't yet included the cross-team or ambiguity-absorbing work a staff loop checks for, which calls for finding genuinely-scoped material or recalibrating the target level, not inventing scope.
